body.en:
A dynamic application needs durable, structured data shared by different requests and users. PHP connects to a database server, sends SQL, reads rows/results, and renders an HTML response. A text file can store feedback, but a relational database adds keys, constraints, efficient queries and controlled concurrent updates.

  • MySQL is a database server; MariaDB is a MySQL-compatible server used by these real executions. MySQLi (MySQL Improved) is PHP's client extension/API; it is not another database server.
  • phpMyAdmin is a PHP web administration interface for managing databases. It is neither MySQL itself nor the connection library used by your own application.
  • The request path is browser → PHP validation/application logic → MySQLi → database → result handling → HTML response. Do not connect browser JavaScript directly to the database with a privileged password.
  • Credentials, SQL and data rules belong on the server. A successful form submission must actually write to the database; a success message alone is not evidence.
  • All Unit 5 program outputs come from PHP 8.4 using mysqlnd/MySQLi and an actual MariaDB server. Each test uses a fresh private database/user; no SQLite emulation or manually invented result rows are used.

<?php
mysqli_report(MYSQLI_REPORT_ERROR | MYSQLI_REPORT_STRICT);

    "localhost", "busbook_app",

  • Explicit mysqli_report(MYSQLI_REPORT_ERROR | MYSQLI_REPORT_STRICT) gives consistent exception-based error handling. Modern PHP commonly enables strict reporting by default, but reference code should make its expectation clear.
  • set_charset('utf8mb4') configures the connection for full Unicode; also create the database/tables with an appropriate charset. A browser's UTF-8 meta tag alone does not configure a database connection.
  • The complete db.php reads environment settings and handles connection failures safely. For local setup, create the database/account as admin, import each schema as admin, then run the app with the less-privileged account.

h.en: phpMyAdmin: Create, Inspect, Run SQL, Export and Delete

body.en:
1. Start the local web/PHP and database services in XAMPP/WAMP/LAMP. Open http://localhost/phpmyadmin where that stack provides it; authenticate with the appropriate local admin account.
  2. Use New / Databases to create a disposable schema with utf8mb4. Select the database in the navigation tree before creating its tables.
  3. Structure shows columns, types, indexes and constraints. Browse shows stored rows. SQL executes entered SQL and displays result/error feedback; menu details vary by version.
  4. Import loads a schema/data SQL file; Export creates a backup. Export before destructive work, and verify you can restore it.
  5. DROP only the intended scratch database/table. Confirm its name before accepting a destructive action. The SQL lab below intentionally deletes its own disposable schema.
-- Disposable schema: never use a real project's name.
CREATE DATABASE busbook_scratch CHARACTER SET utf8mb4;
USE busbook_scratch;
CREATE TABLE books (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  title VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL
);
ALTER TABLE books ADD qty INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;

UPDATE books SET qty=4 WHERE id=1;

  • CREATE/DROP DATABASE and schema alteration require suitable privileges. An ordinary runtime account with only SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE should not administer schemas.
  • To run the PHP scratch lab with the default account, an admin may grant CREATE, ALTER, DROP, SELECT ON busbook_scratch.* to that local lab account; remove administrative privileges when no longer needed.
  • Never expose an unprotected phpMyAdmin/root account on the public internet. Use the host's controlled admin access, strong credentials and suitable access restrictions.

h.en: Designing Tables: Types, Keys, Constraints and DDL

body.en:
CREATE TABLE students (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL,
  email VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  city VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
  marks INT NOT NULL CHECK (marks BETWEEN 0 AND 100)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;
  • INT stores whole numbers; VARCHAR(n) stores bounded text; TEXT stores longer post bodies; DECIMAL(10,2) stores exact fixed-point prices; TIMESTAMP can record creation time. Do not use binary FLOAT for exact money calculations.
  • A PRIMARY KEY uniquely identifies each row and cannot be null. AUTO_INCREMENT generates a new numeric ID; IDs are identifiers, not guaranteed gap-free row counts.
  • NOT NULL, UNIQUE and CHECK enforce server-side rules. Test the target server version's support; these lesson constraints are actually executed on the test server.
  • A FOREIGN KEY links related rows, e.g. movements.stock_id to stock.id. Decide deletion/update behaviour deliberately rather than silently orphaning dependent rows.
  • CREATE TABLE defines structure; ALTER TABLE adds/changes/removes columns or keys; DROP TABLE removes structure and rows. DELETE FROM ... WHERE ... removes selected data, not the table.
  • Constraints complement validation: validate for clear user feedback, then let database rules protect consistency when requests race or another client writes data.

h.en: Executing SELECT and Processing Result Sets

body.en:
<?php
$r = $db->query("SELECT id,name FROM students ORDER BY id");
echo $r->num_rows;
while ($row = $r->fetch_assoc()) {
    echo htmlspecialchars($row["name"]);
}
$r->free();
  • query() with a successful SELECT returns a mysqli_result. A successful INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE through query returns true rather than a row set. With strict reporting, failures throw mysqli_sql_exception.
  • num_rows counts rows in a buffered result. fetch_assoc() returns the next row keyed by column names; null marks exhaustion. fetch_all(MYSQLI_ASSOC) reads all remaining rows as an array.
  • Use explicit columns and stable ORDER BY when order matters. Do not assume rows arrive in insertion order just because a small test happened to do so.
  • free() releases the result; close statements/connections when their work is finished. PHP also cleans up request-bound resources, but explicit lifecycle knowledge matters for long-running work.
  • The procedural program selects two Surat students from a genuine seeded table. Hard-coded constant SQL is safe from value interpolation; any submitted search/filter value should instead be bound.
  • Values stored in a database are not automatically safe HTML. Escape output even if the original source was a trusted-looking form.

h.en: prepare, bind_param, execute and Fetching Prepared Results

body.en:
<?php
$s = $db->prepare(
    "INSERT INTO students(name,email,city,marks) VALUES (?,?,?,?)"
);
$name = "Diya";
$email = "diya@example.test";
$city = "Surat";
$marks = 88;
$s->bind_param("sssi", $name, $email, $city, $marks);
$s->execute();
echo $db->insert_id;
$s->close();
  1. Prepare the SQL template with unquoted ? placeholders in value positions.
  2. Bind variables in placeholder order. Type letters are i integer, d double, s string and b blob. Count and order must match.
  3. Execute using the current bound variable values. bind_param binds by reference; use variables, not temporary literal expressions.
  4. Inspect: INSERT can supply $db->insert_id; writes expose $stmt->affected_rows; SELECT can use get_result() then fetch rows.
  5. Reuse/close: assign new variable values and execute again if appropriate; close the statement after its work.
  • get_result() requires mysqlnd support. Where unavailable, use bind_result($id, $name) followed by fetch() instead. The supplied runtime includes mysqlnd.
  • The INSERT program actually stores Diya and O'Neil, then demonstrates the UNIQUE email constraint rejecting a duplicate. The successful row count remains two; a rejected insert may still consume an auto-increment value.
  • For exact money, validate a decimal string and store it in DECIMAL; the inventory program binds that decimal string as s, avoiding application-side binary floating-point arithmetic.

h.en: CRUD: Create, Read, Update and Delete Safely

body.en:
CRUDSQL patternTypical form behaviour
CreateINSERT INTO posts(title,body) VALUES (?,?)Validated POST, obtain new ID, redirect
ReadSELECT ... WHERE id=?GET listing/detail/search; fetch results
UpdateUPDATE posts SET title=? WHERE id=?Load edit form by GET; save by POST
DeleteDELETE FROM posts WHERE id=?Explicit CSRF-protected POST; never a deleting GET link
  • Validate record IDs as positive integers and check existence where needed. Casting arbitrary input to int is not a substitute for meaningful validation.
  • WHERE is critical: without it, UPDATE/DELETE may alter every row. A prepared statement without the intended WHERE is still logically dangerous.
  • affected_rows is evidence of the last write, not a SELECT count. With default client flags, UPDATE can return zero both for a missing row and for an unchanged value. Check existence separately if the UI must distinguish those cases.
  • On successful writes, use Post/Redirect/Get: send a 303 Location response and exit. The fresh GET lists committed state and reduces refresh resubmission.
  • POST/CSRF prevents some forged or unintended requests; it does not grant permission to edit someone else's data. Add ownership/role checks for a real multi-user application.

h.en: Preventing SQL Injection: Values Are Not SQL Syntax

body.en:
SQL injection occurs when untrusted input is concatenated into SQL and changes the query's structure. A value like missing' OR '1'='1 can turn a supposed exact lookup into an always-true predicate.

<?php
$s = $db->prepare("SELECT id,name FROM contacts WHERE name=?");
$name = $_GET["name"] ?? "";
if (!is_string($name)) {
    http_response_code(400);
    exit("Invalid name.");
}
$s->bind_param("s", $name);
$s->execute();
$rows = $s->get_result()->fetch_all(MYSQLI_ASSOC);
  • Prepared statements keep SQL structure separate from parameter data. The server treats an apostrophe or OR expression in a bound value as data, not as newly supplied SQL syntax.
  • Do not quote the placeholder itself: use WHERE name=?, not a quoted question mark. Do not concatenate a submitted value elsewhere in the same query and assume the prepared part protects it.
  • ? cannot stand for a table name, column name, ASC/DESC keyword or arbitrary SQL clause. Map submitted options through a small allowlist of trusted identifiers/fragments.
  • htmlspecialchars protects HTML output, not SQL. addslashes is not the preferred SQL defence. Even proper SQL escaping requires correct connection encoding and is more error-prone than parameterising values.
  • A bound LIKE value can still contain legitimate LIKE wildcards such as %. That affects search semantics, not SQL structure; escape wildcards separately if the requirement is literal substring matching.
  • The isolated read-only anti-example returns all three seed contacts; the prepared probe returns zero, and a genuine O'Neil lookup returns one. The unsafe query is labelled a lab anti-example and is absent from all four web apps.

title.en: 5.4 Error Handling, Consistency and Application Security

h.en: Database Exceptions, Transactions, Commit and Rollback

body.en:
• Use strict MySQLi reporting and catch mysqli_sql_exception where a known condition needs a specific response. For example, duplicate key error 1062 can become a clear validation message; unrelated failures should still be logged/handled rather than silently ignored.
  • A transaction groups related writes: begin_transaction() → operations → commit() on complete success; rollback() on failure. Use transactional tables such as InnoDB.
  • Stock change + movement log is a useful example: either decrement the quantity and record the movement, or keep neither change. A failure between independent autocommitted writes otherwise leaves inconsistent data.
  • A conditional statement such as UPDATE stock SET qty=qty-? WHERE id=? AND qty>=? checks availability in the write itself. A separate read-then-update without adequate locking can race with another request.
  • The program commits a sale of 2 from 5, rejects a later sale of 9, and verifies the remaining quantity (3) and movement rows (1). Validate positive quantities before processing any stock request.
  • CREATE/ALTER/DROP can cause implicit commits; do not assume DDL will roll back like normal InnoDB row changes. Transactions also do not magically undo external email or other non-database side effects.
  • Keep detailed errors in restricted server logs, not in public HTML. Free result resources and close statements when finished; roll back any pending transaction before propagating an unexpected failure.

h.en: Validation, Escaping, CSRF and Authorisation Are Separate Jobs

body.en:
BoundaryRequired control
Input shape/business rulesValidate IDs, lengths, email, non-negative integer stock, permitted actions and decimal prices.
SQL executionBind values; allowlist structural options; use a least-privileged database account.
HTML outputEscape database/form values with htmlspecialchars, including attributes and textarea content.
State-changing HTTP requestPOST + a server-checked session CSRF token + Post/Redirect/Get after success.
Access to private dataAuthenticate and authorise every applicable request; a CSRF token is not a login.
Deployment/configurationHTTPS, secure session cookies, private secrets, safe public errors, updates and backups.
  • A row read back from the database can contain a stored XSS payload. For a post body use nl2br(htmlspecialchars($body)), not raw HTML rendering.
  • Hidden fields and dropdowns are editable by a client. Check every posted ID/action and re-check permissions on the server.
  • All project writes use CSRF-protected POSTs. Blog, Contacts and To-Do are intentionally local, single-user/admin labs; add the Unit 4 access guard and record-level permissions before public or multi-user use.
  • Inventory includes its own login gate and has no default admin password: ADMIN_HASH must be configured. Its successful login rotates the session ID/token; full logout revokes access.

h.en: Blog Application: Complete Create, Read, Update and Delete (Practical 20)

body.en:
CREATE TABLE posts (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  title VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  body TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
) ENGINE=InnoDB;
  • Create: a POST supplies title/body; validate title 1-100 and body 1-5000 bytes in this reference, execute a prepared INSERT, then redirect.
  • Read: list posts in stable ID order and search titles with a bound LIKE value. All displayed titles/bodies are escaped; newline formatting is applied only after escaping.
  • Update: a GET edit ID loads the existing row into a sticky form; POST validates both input and row existence before a prepared UPDATE.
  • Delete: the per-post form sends a positive ID, action and CSRF token by POST. Delete one matching primary key, then redirect to the updated list.
  • Files: index.php, db.php, web.php, plus the one-time schema SQL. The full code card shows each PHP file; save sections separately.
  • Verify: create BusBook Begins, edit it to Weekend Route Update, search Weekend, then delete it. The genuine transcript ends with Posts: 0.
  • Lengths in these compact references use strlen (byte length); use mb_strlen plus a consistent validation policy when character-count rules for multilingual text are required.

MVC separates responsibilities so changes to HTML do not force changes to SQL. It is an organisation pattern, not a framework you must install.

index.php                 front controller / wiring
db.php                    connection and charset
web.php                   CSRF, validation, HTML helpers
app/Contact.php           MODEL: prepared SQL only
app/ContactController.php CONTROLLER: request handling
views/contacts.php        VIEW: escaped HTML only
schema.sql                one-time admin import
CREATE TABLE contacts (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL,
  email VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL
) ENGINE=InnoDB;
  • Model (Contact): owns prepared database operations: search, find, save and delete. It knows table structure but does not read $_POST or emit HTML.
  • Controller (ContactController): reads the request, validates name/email/ID, checks CSRF, chooses the model operation, redirects after writes, and passes data to the view.
  • View: renders forms and contact rows using escaped values. It does not open connections or run SQL.
  • Front controller: index.php creates the dependencies and calls handle. Constructors receive a connection/model, illustrating a simple OOP design without hidden global dependencies inside the classes.
  • All four requirements are implemented: add, search, update, delete. Name and email search values and every write ID/value are bound parameters.
  • Test O'Neil as legitimate data and an injection-shaped search as literal input. Correct handling is one matching contact for the real name and no broad data disclosure for the probe.

The practical asks for a PHP To-Do application with the help of an AI code-generation tool. The reference here is generated for this lesson, reviewed and really executed; it does not claim that a separate external AI service was used.

CREATE TABLE todos (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  title VARCHAR(150) NOT NULL,
  done TINYINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (done IN (0,1))
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

Example requirement prompt:

Build a small PHP 8/MySQLi To-Do app.
Requirements: add, list, edit, toggle done, delete,
and filter all/pending/done. Use a todos table.
Use prepared values, strict ID validation, server-side
validation, escaped HTML, POST + CSRF for writes,
and Post/Redirect/Get. Separate connection secrets.
Provide schema.sql and a test matrix. Do not use
production credentials or claim unrun tests passed.
  1. Specify: list features, table fields, PHP/MySQLi requirement, safety rules and acceptance tests before requesting code. Do not provide real production credentials.
  2. Inspect: explain each query and request branch. Replace concatenated values, deleting GET links, raw HTML echoes and unchecked IDs; ensure server-side validation exists.
  3. Run: import a fresh schema, configure the connection, open through a PHP server, then test create/edit/toggle/filter/delete against actual stored rows.
  4. Challenge: submit a blank title, forged token, missing ID and unrecognised filter. The reference rejects them and keeps valid state.
  5. Document: retain the prompt, original response, your corrections, screenshots and the observed test results. Be able to explain the code rather than merely copying generated output.
  • The implementation uses a boolean-like done field constrained to 0/1. Toggle updates one ID; all/pending/done filters map to fixed allowlisted SQL fragments.
  • Human review and real execution are necessary even when generated code looks plausible. Never record a test as passed without actually running it.

h.en: Inventory Management: CRUD, Login and Stock Integrity (Practical 23)

body.en:
CREATE TABLE products (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  sku VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL,
  qty INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (qty BETWEEN 0 AND 1000000),
  price DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (price >= 0)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;
  • Products: unique SKU, name, integer quantity and DECIMAL price. Create/update validate every field; list/edit/delete target explicit IDs.
  • Stock operations: sell/restock use positive integers and conditional UPDATEs. Overselling returns 409 without decreasing quantity; restocking also enforces the maximum quantity. Quantity at or below 3 shows a low-stock alert.
  • Authentication: auth.php refuses operation unless ADMIN_HASH is configured. Login uses password_verify; successful authentication rotates the session ID/token. Anonymous requests see login, not product records.
  • Writes: CSRF-protected POSTs and prepared values; duplicate SKU becomes a user-facing validation error instead of a raw database message.
  • Money: validated decimal strings are bound as strings into DECIMAL. This avoids relying on binary floating-point calculations for the displayed price.
  • Local proof: add USB Cable at qty 5, update to 8, sell 6 (qty 2), reject an oversell, restock 3 (qty 5), delete and log out. Test credentials in the transcript are only disposable lab credentials.
  • Hosting is a separate step: the reference has been locally executed, not externally deployed as a live inventory service. Follow the next section to carry out the hosting part on your own PHP-capable account.

h.en: Hosting the Inventory Application: Deployment Checklist

body.en:
1. Choose an appropriate host: supported PHP with mysqli/mysqlnd, a MySQL-compatible database and HTTPS. Static-file hosting, including GitHub Pages, cannot execute PHP or run this database application.
  2. Back up: export schema/data with phpMyAdmin or an appropriate dump tool; retain a restorable local copy. Practise import before changing the deployed database.
  3. Create database/account: import schema using an administrative account, then give the runtime application only the SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE privileges it needs on that database.
  4. Configure secrets privately: set DB_HOST, DB_NAME, DB_USER, DB_PASS and a unique ADMIN_HASH using the hosting/server's environment mechanism. PHP does not automatically load .env. Never place real passwords in a public repository, downloadable SQL backup or source-view endpoint.
  5. Upload files: transfer the required PHP files and confirm paths/case sensitivity. Keep admin-only imports/backups and private configuration outside the public document root where possible.
  6. Enforce HTTPS: make sure the server correctly recognises HTTPS and sends Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite session cookies. Behind a TLS proxy, configure this according to the trusted deployment rather than trusting an arbitrary client-supplied header.
  7. Safe error policy: disable public debug/stack-trace output, log details to restricted server logs and test the friendly failure path with a temporary bad configuration.
  8. Remote smoke test: guest blocked, login succeeds with your own password, CRUD persists after reload, duplicate/negative values fail, oversell does not alter stock, CSRF fails safely and logout revokes direct access.
  9. Maintain: keep PHP/server dependencies updated, rotate credentials when needed, monitor access/errors and regularly test backup restoration.

The lesson's publication makes the study material available in the app. It is not a claim that the inventory PHP/database project itself has been hosted on an external service.

title.en: Transaction: atomic stock change with commit and rollback

code.en:
<?php
// ===== File: stock_transaction.php =====
require __DIR__ . "/db.php";
header("Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8");
function sell(mysqli $db, int $wanted): void {
    if ($wanted <= 0) {
        throw new InvalidArgumentException("Quantity must be positive.");
    }
    $db->begin_transaction();
    try {
        $id = 1;
        $s = $db->prepare("UPDATE stock SET qty=qty-? WHERE id=? AND qty>=?");
        $s->bind_param("iii", $wanted, $id, $wanted);
        $s->execute();
        if ($s->affected_rows !== 1) {
            throw new RuntimeException("Insufficient stock.");
        }
        $s->close();
        $delta = -$wanted;
        $s = $db->prepare("INSERT INTO movements(stock_id,delta) VALUES (?,?)");
        $s->bind_param("ii", $id, $delta);
        $s->execute();
        $s->close();
        $db->commit();
        echo "Committed sale of $wanted.\n";
    } catch (RuntimeException $e) {
        $db->rollback();
        echo "Rolled back: ", $e->getMessage(), "\n";
    } catch (Throwable $e) {
        $db->rollback();
        throw $e;
    }
}
sell($db, 2);
sell($db, 9);
echo "Final qty: ", $db->query("SELECT qty FROM stock WHERE id=1")->fetch_assoc()["qty"], "\n";
echo "Movement rows: ", $db->query("SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM movements")->fetch_assoc()["n"], "\n";

<?php

mysqli_report(MYSQLI_REPORT_ERROR | MYSQLI_REPORT_STRICT);
$host = getenv("DB_HOST") ?: "localhost";
$user = getenv("DB_USER") ?: "busbook_app";

try {

Rolled back: Insufficient stock.

expl.en:
InnoDB groups the stock decrement and audit insert into one unit. A conditional UPDATE prevents selling more than the available quantity; commit keeps both writes, rollback prevents a partial operation. The first sale (2 of 5) succeeds; the second (9 of 3) fails, leaving quantity 3 and one movement. The function rejects non-positive quantities before beginning; real request handlers must also validate submitted integer shape/range. DDL such as CREATE/ALTER often causes implicit commits and is not part of this transaction.

Inventory Manager supports product CRUD, unique SKU, integer quantities, DECIMAL prices, low-stock alerts, atomic sell/restock and authenticated access. auth.php requires an ADMIN_HASH environment value generated with password_hash; it has no built-in default password. Selling 99 when only 2 remain returns 409 and leaves stock unchanged. Prices are bound as validated decimal strings, not binary floating-point arithmetic. q.en: What does MySQLi stand for?

a.en: MySQL Improved: PHP's extension/API for connecting to a MySQL-compatible database and executing queries, including prepared statements.

q.en: MySQL vs phpMyAdmin?

a.en: MySQL is a database server. phpMyAdmin is a web administration interface for it or a compatible server; your own PHP application uses a client API such as MySQLi.

q.en: Which database actually generated this unit's outputs?

a.en: A real MariaDB server through PHP 8.4 mysqlnd/MySQLi. MariaDB is MySQL-compatible; these outputs are not SQLite emulation or hand-written rows.

q.en: Why use a database instead of a feedback text file?

a.en: Structured queries, keys, constraints, shared persistent storage and transactional/concurrent changes become easier to manage reliably.

q.en: Name the usual MySQLi connection arguments.

a.en: Host, username, password and database, with optional port and Unix socket. Keep credentials in private server configuration.

q.en: Why can localhost and 127.0.0.1 behave differently?

a.en: localhost may select a local Unix socket, whereas 127.0.0.1 normally uses TCP. Match the server listener and connection configuration.

q.en: Why call set_charset('utf8mb4')?

a.en: It configures full-Unicode encoding on the database connection. A UTF-8 HTML meta tag does not configure the connection or table charset.

q.en: Object-oriented vs procedural MySQLi?

a.en: They expose the same underlying API in different syntax: $db->query($sql) versus mysqli_query($db,$sql), for example.

q.en: phpMyAdmin Structure vs Browse vs SQL?

a.en: Structure shows columns/indexes/constraints; Browse shows records; SQL runs entered statements and presents their results or errors.

q.en: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE do what?

a.en: Create defines structure, alter changes it, and drop removes the table including its data. These are DDL operations.

q.en: DELETE FROM vs DROP TABLE?

a.en: DELETE removes selected rows while keeping table structure; DROP removes the structure and its rows. Be certain of the target and back up first.

q.en: Primary key, UNIQUE and AUTO_INCREMENT?

a.en: A primary key uniquely identifies a non-null row; UNIQUE rejects duplicate values under its rules; AUTO_INCREMENT generates numeric identifiers, not gap-free row numbers.

q.en: What does query() return for SELECT versus a successful UPDATE?

a.en: SELECT returns mysqli_result; an UPDATE through query returns true on success. With strict reporting, failures throw rather than being ordinary successful results.

q.en: What does fetch_assoc do at the end of a result?

a.en: It returns the next associative row each time and null when no rows remain. The keys correspond to selected column names or aliases.

q.en: num_rows vs affected_rows?

a.en: num_rows counts buffered result rows from a SELECT; affected_rows reports the last write's affected-row count, subject to operation/client flags.

q.en: What is insert_id?

a.en: The generated auto-increment ID from the last applicable insert on that connection. It is not the number of records in the table.

q.en: The normal prepared-statement sequence?

a.en: prepare the SQL template; bind variables; execute; fetch SELECT results or inspect write evidence; close when finished.

q.en: What are the bind_param type letters?

a.en: i integer, d double, s string and b blob. The type-string length/order and variables must match the placeholders.

q.en: What does binding by reference mean?

a.en: The statement uses the current values of its bound variables at execute time. Change those variables and execute again to reuse it; bind variables rather than temporary expressions.

q.en: Why must the question-mark placeholder not be quoted?

a.en: The unquoted question mark marks a parameter position. Quoting it makes it a literal SQL string rather than that parameter placeholder.

q.en: What if get_result is unavailable?

a.en: get_result requires mysqlnd. Bind output variables with bind_result and loop fetch instead, or deploy with mysqlnd support.

q.en: Why is WHERE critical in UPDATE and DELETE?

a.en: Without the intended predicate the statement can affect all rows. Parameterisation does not repair a missing or logically wrong WHERE clause.

q.en: Does UPDATE affected_rows=0 always mean no matching ID?

a.en: No. With default client flags it can also mean the matching row already had those values. Check existence separately if the UI needs that distinction.

q.en: Should the production runtime account have CREATE/DROP privileges?

a.en: Normally not for a CRUD application. Import/migrate schemas with an appropriate admin account, then grant only the runtime privileges actually required.

q.en: What is SQL injection?

a.en: Untrusted input is incorporated into SQL syntax and changes the query structure, potentially disclosing or changing unintended data.

q.en: How does a prepared parameter prevent value-based injection?

a.en: It keeps the SQL template separate from the bound value, so quotes or OR clauses in that value remain literal data rather than new SQL syntax.

q.en: Can a parameter stand for a table or column name?

a.en: No. Use a controlled mapping/allowlist of trusted identifiers, sort directions or clauses. Bind ordinary values separately.

q.en: Does htmlspecialchars prevent SQL injection?

a.en: No. It escapes HTML output. Prepared SQL values prevent SQL injection; they do not automatically escape the value when rendering HTML.

q.en: Does a bound LIKE value make percent signs literal?

a.en: No. Percent/underscore can still have LIKE wildcard semantics inside the value. That is search behaviour, not SQL injection; escape wildcards separately if literal matching is required.

q.en: Is a CSRF token the same as authentication?

a.en: No. It helps verify request origin/integrity for a session; login and authorisation decide who may access or change the data.

q.en: Why use POST and a redirect for mutations?

a.en: GET should not delete or otherwise mutate records. A validated CSRF-protected POST performs the change, then 303/GET displays stored state and reduces refresh resubmission.

q.en: What do commit and rollback do?

a.en: commit keeps a completed transaction's related changes; rollback undoes its uncommitted transactional row changes after failure.

q.en: Why use InnoDB, and can DDL be rolled back like row writes?

a.en: InnoDB supports these transactions. CREATE/ALTER/DROP can trigger implicit commits, so do not assume DDL participates like ordinary transactional row updates.

q.en: Why check availability inside the stock UPDATE?

a.en: A conditional UPDATE with qty >= amount checks and changes stock atomically. A separate read-then-write can race unless adequate concurrency control is used.

q.en: Why use DECIMAL for prices?

a.en: It stores exact fixed-point decimal amounts; binary floating-point can introduce rounding surprises. The reference validates and binds price strings into DECIMAL.

q.en: How should duplicate key error 1062 and unexpected errors be handled?

a.en: Recognise the known duplicate case and show a clear validation message; log unexpected details securely and return a safe generic failure instead of exposing raw database messages.

title.en: MVC, Projects, AI Review and Hosting

q.en: What is MVC?

a.en: Model-View-Controller: a separation of data access, presentation and request/application coordination. A small PHP MVC app does not require a framework.

q.en: What belongs in the Contact model?

a.en: Prepared database operations such as search/find/save/delete. It should not read $_POST or emit HTML.

q.en: What belongs in the controller?

a.en: Read and validate HTTP input, check CSRF/permissions, call the appropriate model method, choose a redirect or pass data to a view.

q.en: What belongs in the view?

a.en: Forms and escaped HTML output. It should not open database connections or execute SQL.

q.en: Why pass a model/connection through a constructor?

a.en: Dependencies become explicit and replaceable, rather than hidden global state inside every method; the front controller wires them together.

q.en: Name the four Blog CRUD actions in Practical 20.

a.en: Create a validated post, list/read/search stored posts, load and save an edit, and delete one primary key using a CSRF-protected POST.

q.en: What evidence should an AI-assisted To-Do practical record?

a.en: The requirement prompt, generated draft, your review/corrections, and actually observed add/edit/toggle/filter/delete and negative-test results. Never claim unrun tests passed.

q.en: Why is the To-Do filter allowlisted?

a.en: The all/pending/done key selects a fixed trusted SQL fragment. Arbitrary submitted SQL clauses are not concatenated into the query.

q.en: Which Inventory values must be validated?

a.en: SKU shape/uniqueness, name length, non-negative integer quantity, decimal price precision, positive stock-change amount and explicit record ID, alongside session/CSRF checks.

q.en: Why does Inventory require ADMIN_HASH?

a.en: There is no built-in default admin password. The operator configures a hash of a unique chosen password; login checks it with password_verify and starts authenticated access.

q.en: Can this PHP inventory run on static hosting such as GitHub Pages?

a.en: No. It needs a PHP-capable server with MySQLi/mysqlnd and a compatible database. Publishing study-material JSON/HTML is different from hosting that database application.

q.en: What proves a successful remote deployment?

a.en: Remote guest/login/CRUD/validation/oversell/logout smoke tests over HTTPS, correctly configured private credentials, safe errors and a tested backup/restore process; local execution alone is not proof.
